issue_context.title: Config binder generator generates uncompilable code when a private nested type is used
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-extensions-configuration See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
This compiles fine: ```C# using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration; internal class Program { private static void Main() { } private static C Foo(IConfiguration configuration) { C c = new(); configuration.Bind(c); return c; } internal sealed class C { public int Value { get; set; } } } ``` but changing: ```C# internal sealed class C ``` to ```C# private sealed class C ``` produces an error about `C` being inaccessible, as the generator emits code into another class that tries to access that property.
Author: stephentoub
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-Extensions-Configuration`
Milestone: -
I'd say the resolution would be to emit a diagnostic & omit code to support inaccessible members.

review_comments: What about `internal` members that are in referenced assemblies?

We shouldn't be seeing those in this routine. This method is for root binding types only. `InternalsVisibleTo` usage is interesting but the current logic handles the scenario.

For transitive types - the generator only inspects public properties. The compiler would have complained if a type had a public member whose declared type is internal. So we don't have to guard against that explicitly
My point is we should try to use IsSymbolAccessibleWithin rather than attempt to reimplement accessibility resolution.
Yeah I fully intended to use it; will do if possible per discussion here https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/91657#discussion_r1318574410.

The issue as described in https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/54185 hasn't been fixed in Roslyn 3.11 (and won't be fixed). We should keep this comment (and possibly with a TODO explaining that we should remove it once Roslyn 3.11 support is removed).

>!IsAccessibleFromGenBinders(type) || [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=20&length=36)

Is this mean we'll have a difference between the source gen and the runtime in such cases?

In a sense... we won't generate a replacement interceptor for the invocation, meaning that it will always fallback to reflection. AOT users will get a warning and the fix would be to adjust the visibility.

Will the users get anything to help them tell them what to do? I mean how the users know the source gen didn't handle it because of the class visibility? Would it make sense to produce info diagnostics for this one? It doesn't have to be part of this PR.

Yup, should have mentioned this -- we produce a diagnostic for all `false` returns of the calling `IsValidRootConfigType(ITypeSymbol?)` method. Hence, we need the suppressions below:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/91657/files#diff-81e6cde105e57e3f3b3a0107c173264b96aee943a0faa6b8f1bd72d7a57a43a3R333-R343
I'm not comfortable making cross-cutting changes in RC2 backports. To minimize risk, we should be making targeted changes even if it results in temporary code duplication.

I don't think this algorithm should live in shared code. It should be specific to each application since changing the algorithm in the future is a potential breaking change, and what we have here isn't perfect (i.e. it is subject to ambiguity in nested types, nested generics or types in different namespaces).

Okay I'll revert in this PR. 

---

For 9.0, I still think we should at least have the separate implementations live next to each other so they can be kept in sync. If one generator makes an important improvement, then we would address the other one if needed.

IMO this would also increase discoverability of common concerns when handling type graphs in source-gen (formatting identifiers, visibility checks, formatting names with special syntax e.g. `@int` etc.) Authors would know to check the shared code dir for helper APIs that already exist, that they might not need to rewrite.

Changing the identifier generation algorithm can be a potential source breaking change, since user code referencing source generated members from earlier SG versions could fail to compile.

Even if the new logic is equivalent to the old one, this will get backported to RC2 and it's not clear to me why we should take the risk this late.

Couldn't you use `IsSymbolAccessibleWithin` instead?

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.compilation.issymbolaccessiblewithin?view=roslyn-dotnet-4.6.0
I don't have a "within" symbol. The symbol would be the generated binder extension class which doesn't exist yet.
Couldn't you use another type symbol in the same assembly as a proxy for the one that will be generated?
It should be possible to use the current IAssemblySymbol as the 'within' parameter although I haven't tested that myself.
Yes I considered the proxy approach. It didn't feel deterministic on first thought, but yes it would be a correct/better check. I'll also try using the assembly symbol.

Using a proxy would work in the common case, but we'd need to account for the assembly possibly having just one (e.g. a singular, simple target-config POCO with primitive fields). Any handwritten fallback would have a vastly different impl.

Comparing with assembly doesn't work - nested privates aren't visible.

> Comparing with assembly doesn't work - nested privates aren't visible.

Are any of the types being generated nested within user-defined types? If not, I would expect its visibility to be equivalent to that of the assembly?

> Comparing with assembly doesn't work - nested privates aren't visible.

I tried it again; the assembly check works. Must have not used the `!` operator when I tried. Thanks.
